description: Kitchener's army, DORA, the role of women, propaganda and growing disillusionment with the war.
content_html:
Britain Goes to War: Recruitment and Kitchener’s Army

When Britain declared war on Germany on 4 August 1914, the British Army was small by European standards — around 250,000 regular troops, compared to the millions of conscripts in the German and French armies. The Secretary of State for War, Field Marshal Lord Kitchener, was almost unique among British leaders in predicting that the war would last for years, not months. He immediately called for a mass volunteer army of 100,000 men. Within two months he had received more than 750,000 volunteers.

Recruitment was driven by a powerful propaganda campaign. The most famous image of the war was Alfred Leete’s 1914 poster of Kitchener pointing directly at the viewer with the slogan “Your Country Needs You.” Recruitment offices opened across the country. Social pressure was enormous: women were encouraged to give white feathers to young men seen out of uniform as symbols of cowardice.

Key Fact

Pals battalions were created to encourage men to enlist by promising they could serve alongside friends and neighbours. Towns and factories raised their own units. When a Pals battalion suffered heavy casualties — as many did on the first day of the Somme in July 1916 — whole communities lost an entire generation at once.

The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA), 1914

The Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) was passed in August 1914 and subsequently extended several times. It gave the government extraordinary powers over everyday life. Under DORA the government could:

  • Censor newspapers and restrict reporting of military operations.
  • Requisition buildings, land and factories for war purposes.
  • Restrict pub opening hours and control the alcohol content of beer to maintain worker productivity.
  • Prosecute anyone whose actions were deemed to undermine the war effort, including pacifists and conscientious objectors.

DORA represented a dramatic expansion of state power into areas previously considered private. The government took control of the railways, coal mines and munitions production. Daylight saving time was introduced in 1916 under DORA to extend working hours. Citizens could be prosecuted for flying a kite, lighting a bonfire on the beach, or discussing naval movements in public.

Conscription, 1916

Volunteer recruitment began to fall short of the army’s needs by late 1915. The Military Service Act of January 1916 introduced conscription for single men aged 18 to 41; it was extended to married men in May 1916. This was the first time in modern British history that men had been legally compelled to serve in the armed forces. A system of tribunals was established to hear applications for exemption on grounds of conscience, health or essential employment. Those who refused to serve on grounds of conscience were known as conscientious objectors; some performed non-combatant duties, others were imprisoned, and a small number were sent to France and threatened with execution.

The war transformed women’s employment. As men enlisted, women moved into jobs previously closed to them: as bus conductresses, delivery drivers, police officers, civil servants and bank clerks. Most significant was their role in industry. Munitionettes worked in munitions factories making shells, fuses and explosives, often handling toxic chemicals such as TNT that turned their skin yellow, earning them the nickname “canary girls.” By 1918 around 800,000 women were employed in munitions. Women also served in the Women’s Land Army (farming) and as nurses close to the front line.

The government used propaganda to sustain public support for the war. Propaganda took many forms: recruitment posters, cinema newsreels (the Battle of the Somme film of 1916 was watched by an estimated 20 million people within six weeks), newspaper reports censored to downplay defeats and emphasise victories, and stories about German atrocities in Belgium, some of which were exaggerated or fabricated. The government established the War Propaganda Bureau at Wellington House in 1914, staffed by prominent writers including Arthur Conan Doyle, Rudyard Kipling and Thomas Hardy.

By 1917 the propaganda effort was increasingly strained. Casualty lists published in local newspapers contradicted optimistic official statements. War poetry by soldiers such as Siegfried Sassoon and Wilfred Owen circulated privately and began to reach wider audiences, presenting a very different picture of the war than official communications.

Growing Disillusionment

The early enthusiasm of 1914 gave way to a more complex public mood by 1916–1917. The Battle of the Somme’s casualties, food shortages caused by the German submarine campaign, and the endless casualty lists in newspapers eroded initial patriotism. In 1917 Siegfried Sassoon wrote a public statement refusing to return to the front, condemning the war as “a war of aggression and conquest” being prolonged by those with “the power to end it.” He was not court-martialled but declared to have shell shock and sent to a hospital. Wilfred Owen, who met Sassoon there, wrote much of his greatest anti-war poetry at Craiglockhart hospital in Edinburgh.

Key Fact

By the end of the war in November 1918, approximately 750,000 British soldiers had been killed and around 1.7 million wounded. The scale of loss permanently altered British society and created the “lost generation” narrative that shaped interwar politics and culture.
exam_tip_html: For questions on the Home Front, be precise about the timeline: early enthusiasm and voluntary recruitment (1914–1915) shifted to conscription (1916) and growing disillusionment (1917–1918). For ‘Source Utility’ questions, a recruitment poster is very useful for showing government propaganda methods but less useful for understanding the reality of soldiers’ experiences — always link your assessment to the specific enquiry question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Kitchener’s mass volunteer army raised over 750,000 men by October 1914. Pals battalions encouraged community enlistment but devastated specific towns when they suffered heavy casualties. Conscription was introduced in January 1916.
  • DORA (1914) gave the government sweeping powers: press censorship, restricted pub hours, requisition of industry. Propaganda — posters, newsreels, censored press — sustained the war effort.
  • Women took on vital roles in munitions, farming and nursing. By 1917 growing disillusionment — expressed in war poetry by Owen and Sassoon — challenged official narratives, though popular support held until the armistice in November 1918.

practice_questions.text: Describe one feature of the Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) of 1914.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks for a developed point. Example: DORA gave the government power to censor newspapers (1), restricting reporting of military operations and information that could aid the enemy (1). Mastering: accurate feature with precise supporting detail.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the role of women on the Home Front during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Award 2 marks per feature. Feature examples: munitionettes in factories making shells and explosives (handling toxic TNT — 'canary girls'); Women's Land Army working on farms; nursing close to the front line; taking on jobs as bus conductresses, delivery drivers, police officers, civil servants; around 800,000 women in munitions by 1918. Mastering: two precise features with accurate detail.

practice_questions.text: Explain one reason why the British government introduced conscription in January 1916.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Volunteer recruitment had fallen short of the army's needs by late 1915; the enormous casualties of 1914–1915 could not be replaced by volunteers alone; the campaign for Kitchener's army had successfully recruited over a million men but numbers were declining; the Military Service Act was necessary to maintain army strength for the campaigns planned for 1916, including the Somme. Secure (3–4): clear cause with development. Developing (1–2): simple identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain one consequence of the government's use of propaganda during the First World War.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (5–6): Government propaganda (posters, censored press, the Somme film watched by ~20 million) sustained public support for the war in the critical early years; it shaped public understanding of the enemy (German atrocity stories) and encouraged enlistment; however, when casualty lists contradicted optimistic propaganda by 1917, the gap between official narrative and reality fuelled disillusionment and anti-war sentiment. Secure (3–4): clear consequence with development. Developing (1–2): simple statement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the significance of growing disillusionment with the war in Britain by 1917.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (7–8): At the time: Sassoon's public protest in 1917 and the circulation of anti-war poetry by Owen challenged the official narrative; food shortages and casualty lists eroded morale; the government had to use DORA to suppress dissent. Over time: the anti-war tradition shaped interwar pacifism and the 'never again' mood of the 1920s–30s; war poetry by Owen and Sassoon became central to twentieth-century cultural understanding of the war; the 'lost generation' narrative influenced the decision not to resist Hitler more forcefully in the 1930s. Secure (5–6): both dimensions with development. Developing (3–4): mainly one dimension. Emerging (1–2): simple assertion.

practice_questions.text: 'Propaganda was the main reason why public support for the war was maintained in Britain until 1918.' How far do you agree?
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Agree and disagree, substantiated, overall judgement. Agree: propaganda shaped public understanding at a critical time; censorship prevented accurate reporting of defeats; the Somme film maintained public engagement; white feather campaigns and social pressure enforced conformity. Disagree: genuine patriotism and belief in the justice of Britain's cause (Belgian neutrality, German militarism) were real motivations; the practical difficulty of opposing a war once it had started (legal penalties under DORA) was a constraint; many families were invested through the loss of relatives and had personal reasons to want victory. Balanced: propaganda was essential but worked because it reinforced existing beliefs — when reality diverged too far (by 1917) it began to fail. Secure (7–9): argument both ways. Developing (4–6): limited. Emerging (1–3): one-sided.

knowledge_checks.q: What was the main purpose of the Defence of the Realm Act (DORA) of 1914?
options: To introduce conscription for all men over 18
To give the government sweeping powers to control civilian life in wartime
To ban trade unions from striking during the war
To nationalise all British banks for the war effort

glossary_terms.definition: Battalions recruited from men of the same town, workplace or social group who enlisted together on the promise of serving together; their destruction in battle devastated entire communities.
The 1914 Act that gave the government sweeping powers to control many aspects of civilian life in wartime Britain, including press censorship, restriction of pub hours, and direction of industry.
Compulsory military service, introduced in Britain in January 1916 when volunteer recruitment proved insufficient to replace battlefield losses.
Women employed in munitions factories during the First World War, handling explosive materials in dangerous conditions essential to the war effort.
Information, often selective or misleading, used by governments to shape public opinion — especially in wartime.

items.description: Continues the story through the Western Front, covering the human cost of the war and the pressures that produced conscription and disillusionment by 1916–17.

items.description: The IWM's channel features eyewitness accounts, archive footage and short documentaries on the Home Front, women's roles and First World War recruitment.

items.title: Testament of Youth (2014)
items.description: Powerful drama based on Vera Brittain's memoir, showing the impact of the First World War on the Home Front, women's war work and the devastation of the 'lost generation'.

items.title: Oh! What a Lovely War (1969)
items.description: Richard Attenborough's satirical film of the stage musical that challenged the 'lions led by donkeys' narrative, using music-hall numbers to expose the human cost of propaganda and command failures.

items.title: IWM: Pals Battalions
items.description: Imperial War Museums article explaining how Pals battalions were raised, the social bonds that made them effective recruiters, and the devastating community impact of their losses at the Somme.

items.title: IWM: Did the First World War Transform Women's Lives?
items.description: IWM analysis of women's wartime roles — munitionettes, the Women's Land Army, nursing — and whether the war produced lasting change or simply a temporary shift.

items.title: Spartacus Educational: Defence of the Realm Act (DORA)
items.description: Detailed topic page on DORA's provisions, its expansion through the war, and the range of activities it restricted — from pub hours to press censorship.

items.title: The National Archives: Britain 1906–1918
items.description: Source-based education resource using primary documents from the National Archives to explore social reform, the war effort and the Home Front.

items.title: IWM: Conscientious Objectors in Their Own Words
items.description: First-hand accounts from men who refused to fight on grounds of conscience, exploring the moral and legal pressures they faced under DORA and the Military Service Act.

items.title: Spartacus Educational: Women and the First World War
items.description: Topic page covering women's employment in munitions, the Women's Land Army, nursing and the social changes brought by the war.

items.title: The National Archives: Writing War, Writing Peace
items.description: Primary source resource exploring how soldiers, poets and propagandists wrote about the First World War — ideal context for comparing official propaganda with anti-war literature.
